children: By Rhiannon Hoyle
When Electroflow Technologies raised its seed round a year ago, the lithium startup was riding the boom for batteries to power electric vehicles.
As it opens Series A talks this week, the San Bruno, Calif.-based company has a new force driving demand: batteries to back up data centers and electricity grids.

The $1 trillion race to build data centers has become a boon for batteries, as hyperscalers increasingly turn to so-called energy storage systems, or ESS, to provide backup power and respond to spikes in electricity demand. The construction frenzy has offset a slackening in the pace of electric-vehicle sales.

Electroflow, which aims to make it cheaper and easier to get lithium for batteries from salty water within the U.S., wants to raise $25 million in its Series A funding round, said co-founder and Chief Executive Eric McShane.

Electroflow says it can extract lithium from brine and convert it into a lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, cathode material in a three-step process-down from roughly 10 steps using traditional methods. LFP batteries dominate large-scale energy storage.

"A year ago, our early demand driver was EV battery applications," said McShane. "Now, the focus is squarely on data-center and grid energy storage system battery applications. Demand for EV use cases is a distant second."

Electroflow last year raised $10 million in its seed round, which was led by Union Square Ventures and Voyager Ventures. Fifty Years and Harpoon Ventures, who joined a $2.8 million pre-seed a year before that, also participated.
Since then, energy-storage system cell shipments have surged, Morgan Stanley analysts said in a recent note. "ESS has emerged as the key demand growth driver for lithium," the bank said.
That demand has helped pull lithium prices out of the doldrums.

A key China price for lithium carbonate-a form of lithium produced by Electroflow in the first step of its process-was $23,150 a metric ton on Sept. 2, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That compares with $10,900 a year ago, and less than $9,000 earlier in 2025.
The price of LFP cathode also nearly doubled over the past year, according to Benchmark.
Electroflow wants to use cash from the planned Series A to upsize the electrochemical cell stack it uses to pull lithium from brines, and significantly increase its LFP output.
It aims to produce the cathode material at an annualized rate of about 300 tons, McShane said. Its current output rate is between five and 10 tons a year.

"LFP batteries are great for data centers because they can be charged from the grid during low-price off-peak hours and discharged during high-price peak hours," said McShane. "They're also very safe, have a long cycle life, and can respond quickly to spiky loads."
Electroflow hopes to gain from a shift by venture-capital firms to physical technologies and materials from software, as investors seek new ways to wager on the artificial-intelligence boom.

A year ago during Electroflow's seed round, McShane observed an increase in investor appetite for deep tech, hardware-focused companies from the year prior's pre-seed, he said. "We expect that appetite has only grown now," said McShane.

However, the pace of energy storage system adoption is expected to slow in coming years, and batteries based on sodium rather than lithium are likely to gain in popularity, according to Morgan Stanley.

Fresh clouds also have emerged over the trajectory of demand for battery materials after Caixin recently reported China had temporarily suspended construction of new projects for manufacturing energy-storage batteries, pending a year-end review of industry capacity. Across the U.S., data-center developers face growing community pushback.

American critical minerals companies have benefited from U.S. ambitions to develop domestic sources of metals like lithium, which is today mostly processed in China. American battery manufacturers face increasingly stringent domestic sourcing requirements for Inflation Reduction Act tax credits.

Electroflow recently received a small investment from Houston oil-services giant Halliburton, McShane said. He declined to comment on the size of the investment, but said the sum will be treated as separate to the Series A raise.

Halliburton Labs said Electroflow's process has the potential to unlock low-concentration brine resources and help strengthen North America's battery supply chain. It said it would work with Electroflow to help the startup scale and deploy its technology.
For Electroflow, the race to build data centers isn't all good news.

In its search for a warehouse to scale up its factory, the startup often finds itself competing with data centers for suitable properties, said McShane. He said the company also has been told that power upgrades to buildings are expected to take over two years in some areas due to long interconnection queues from the build-out.

Its biggest immediate challenge is finding contractors, as the boom has created a shortage of skilled tradespeople. "If they're building something for a data center, we're probably not their highest priority at that point," McShane said.
